title: SULEJMANOV v. "THE FORMER YUGOSLAV REPUBLIC OF MACEDONIA"
summary: In the case of Sulejmanov v. "the former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia," the applicant, Mr. Demir Sulejmanov, was a Roma man from Štip, represented posthumously by his sisters after his death. The case focused on the vulnerability of Roma individuals to police violence and racially motivated abuse, highlighting the specific harm of ill-treatment and the lack of effective investigation or remedy, allegedly aggravated by anti-Roma prejudice. On 13 March 1998, Mr. Sulejmanov and a Roma friend were stopped by police near Balvan on suspicion of theft. According to his account, they were immediately beaten by police, subjected to racist insults such as “There is no water for gypsies!” and further assaulted at the police station, resulting in a broken arm. The authorities disputed the extent of the violence but confirmed some altercation involving the sheep owner. Despite medical evidence of injury, Mr. Sulejmanov’s complaints of police brutality and discrimination were not effectively investigated by national authorities. The European Court of Human Rights examined the case under Articles 3 (prohibition of inhuman or degrading treatment), 13 (right to an effective remedy), and 14 (prohibition of discrimination), but ultimately found parts of the application inadmissible. This case is significant as it illustrates the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller communities face in seeking justice for police abuse, reflecting broader patterns of marginalisation in post-communist Europe.
